analysis.one_liner: Requires Wall Street's self-regulator to pay investors arbitration awards that brokers never paid.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee: after one hearing in June 2018, the Senate Banking Committee took no further action and no vote was ever held.
analysis.plain_summary: When an investor wins an arbitration case against a broker, the award is supposed to be paid. Sometimes it isn't, and the investor can spend years chasing money from a firm that lost fair and square. This bill would force the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority (FINRA), Wall Street's self-regulatory body, to create a fund that pays investors the full amount of any arbitration award confirmed by a court but left unpaid. The fund would be filled first from fines paid by brokers, with reserves drawn from the industry rather than from investors, and FINRA would have to publish an annual public list naming every firm and broker with unpaid awards.
analysis.who_benefits: Investors who won their arbitration cases against a brokerage firm or broker, got a court to confirm the award, and then watched the firm simply not pay. They would be made whole by the relief fund instead of being left to collect from a party that had every incentive to stall. All investors indirectly benefit from the public naming of firms that stiff them, because it creates a real consequence for not paying.

how_it_helps.text: FINRA must establish a relief fund that pays investors the full value of arbitration awards issued in their favor against FINRA-regulated brokers, once a court has confirmed the award in a final, unappealable order and it remains unpaid.

The fund cannot cap what an investor may recover and cannot bar any investor from filing a claim, and FINRA must keep enough reserves to cover even a year with an unusually high number of unpaid awards.
The money must come from the brokerage industry, first from penalties paid by brokers and then from reserves FINRA maintains from firms — not from investors.

FINRA must publish an annual public report naming each firm or broker with an unpaid award, the amount owed, the claims involved, the payment deadline, and whether it was ever paid — or explain why not.
If FINRA drags its feet on writing the fund's rules, it must pay valid claims directly out of its own general budget.

analysis.who_pays: Brokerage firms and individual brokers, through the penalties and mandatory industry reserves that fund the relief fund, plus the cost of heightened public disclosure. Some of that cost would likely flow to customers through higher fees or compliance costs. FINRA itself bears the administrative burden and the risk of paying claims from its general budget if it fails to write rules on time.

drawbacks.text: The funding obligation is open-ended: the bill bars any cap on awards and requires reserves sufficient for even a spike in unpaid awards, which is a heavy and somewhat unpredictable liability for the industry — costs that brokerage customers may ultimately see in fees.

The fund effectively socializes some losses: when a broker who defrauded investors has no assets to pay, the bill makes the industry's collective fund pay instead, so honest firms and their customers share the cost of the worst actors.

The bill relies on FINRA — the very self-regulator whose members' nonpayment created the problem — to design and run the fund, giving the industry's own overseer broad discretion over sources of funds, claim procedures, and timelines.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core promise is straightforward: if a neutral arbitrator and a court both ruled that an investor is owed money, the investor gets paid. That is a real protection for ordinary investors, and the public naming of firms that don't pay addresses a problem that otherwise carries little consequence. The honest costs are that the funding is uncapped and industry-wide, and that the industry's own regulator keeps substantial discretion over how the fund works. On balance the bill's benefits outweigh its costs for the people it covers, though a better-designed version might include clearer limits and stronger outside oversight of FINRA's implementation.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Banking Committee, got one hearing in June 2018, and then sat there while Congress adjourned — no committee vote, no floor vote, nothing.

narrative.text: Sen. Elizabeth Warren introduced the bill in the Senate on March 6, 2018.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs the same day.
The Banking Committee held a hearing on the bill on June 28, 2018 (printed as S.Hrg. 115-406).
Two senators, one Republican and one Democrat, cosponsored the bill.
No further action was ever taken: the committee never voted on the bill, and the Senate never considered it before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.
The bill would have required FINRA to compensate investors for the full value of arbitration awards confirmed in court but left unpaid by regulated brokers.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brokerage firms and brokers who win cases and then don't pay, because the status quo — where an unpaid arbitration award costs them little — stayed in place. FINRA also kept full discretion over how (or whether) to handle unpaid awards.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Brokers who don't pay their awards

for.name: Sen. Elizabeth Warren
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and shepherded it to a committee hearing.

against.name: Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: Held one hearing in June 2018 and then took no further action — no markup, no vote — for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Sen. Mike Crapo
against.what_they_did: As committee chairman, never brought the bill to a committee vote after the single June 2018 hearing.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor was a Democrat joined by one Republican and one Democratic cosponsor, and the bill was never voted on by either chamber, so no roll-call record exists.

industries.industry: Brokerage firms and brokers regulated by FINRA
industries.note: The bill would have required the industry, through penalties and mandatory reserves, to pay arbitration awards its members had refused to pay, and to be publicly named when they didn't. Today, failing to pay an award carries little cost; the bill would have made nonpayment expensive and visible.

The bill preserves FINRA's role as Wall Street's self-regulator but forces it to run a relief fund, disclose delinquent firms by name, and pay claims from its own budget if it fails to write rules. It expands FINRA's obligations while keeping it in charge of implementation.
